record_identity.title: One participant's authority treated as sufficient for another participant's capture or processing

summary: A multi-party authority failure in which a participant, organiser, host, account holder, deployer, tool user, or other person with access to a shared interaction introduces or operates an AI capture, transcription, recording, analysis, or comparable processing system and the system treats that person's authority, account status, invitation, public link, or tool use as sufficient authority over another participant's identifiable contribution. The failure is not that multi-party capture exists; many meeting, classroom, conference, clinical, workplace, and service contexts legitimately require capture of other participants. The failure is the absence of an independently adequate authority, notice, consent, legal basis, or other governance condition for the affected participant and the specific processing at issue.
why_it_matters_to_CAM: Multi-human systems require participant-aware authority rather than a single-user or single-access permission model. One person's choice to use an AI notetaker may legitimately establish the tool's presence in a workflow while remaining insufficient to settle the rights and authority state of every other person captured. WebinarTV adds a distinct but structurally aligned manifestation: technical discoverability or access to a meeting or webinar link can be treated as sufficient authority to capture and republish the contributions of all participants. The required diligence rises with vulnerability and consequence, including where minors, biometric voice or image data, confidential professional material, health information, protected classes, recovery groups, or other sensitive contexts are involved. Public availability or attendance can alter the authority analysis but should not operate as an automatic permission bit for every form of capture or processing.
evidence_confidence: cross-vendor incident-database and journalistic evidence; several underlying litigation allegations remain unresolved, while WebinarTV reporting independently corroborates the broader participant-authority mechanism

source_records.source_title: Incident 1650: Otter.ai Notetaker Allegedly Recorded Meeting Conversations Without Participants' Informed Consent and Used Data for AI Training
source_records.model_or_algorithm: AI speech-to-text and meeting transcription system
source_records.deployment_context: Virtual workplace meetings involving multiple participants where an AI notetaker was introduced into Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, or comparable meeting environments.
source_records.source_context: AIID records allegations that Otter.ai captured private meeting conversations without every participant's informed consent. The same incident record also alleges downstream use for AI training; FM-0073 relies only on the participant-authority and capture aspect, while secondary-use training authority is separated into FM-0074.
source_records.relevance_note: Supports the recurring mechanism that one participant's use of a meeting tool can affect non-user participants whose authority state is not necessarily established by the tool user's own account or consent.

jurisdictional_context.sector: cross-sector multi-party AI capture and processing

contextual_relations.rationale: FM-0073 concerns whether authority from one participant, organiser or access holder validly extends to another person's capture or processing. FM-0074 concerns whether an authorised primary use of data validly extends to a materially different secondary purpose such as model training. Either can occur without the other.

FM-0056 concerns technical access or reachability being mistaken for authority. FM-0073 instead concerns transposition of one human participant's, organiser's or access holder's authority onto another affected human participant.

failure_mode_definition: A failure mode in which authority held or asserted by one participant, organiser, host, account holder, deployer, tool user, or other person with technical access to introduce or operate an AI capture, transcription, recording, analysis, biometric-processing, or comparable system is treated as sufficient authority over another affected participant's identifiable contribution without independently establishing the authority, notice, consent, legal basis, representative authority, or other governance condition required for that participant and processing context. The failure does not prohibit multi-party capture. It requires participant-aware authority resolution proportionate to the context, the type of processing, the sensitivity of the contribution, and the rights or vulnerabilities of the people affected.
failure_threshold: The threshold is met when: (1) a multi-party interaction contains identifiable contributions from more than one human; (2) one participant, organiser, host, account holder, deployer, tool user or technically capable third party introduces or operates an AI system that captures or materially processes the interaction; (3) another participant's identifiable speech, image, biometric representation, text, behaviour, or contribution is captured or materially processed; (4) the system or deployer relies on the invoking person's authority, account status, invitation, public link, technical access or tool use as sufficient authority for the affected participant; and (5) the authority state applicable to that participant has not been independently established to the level required for the context and use. Public accessibility, attendance, visibility or technical reachability may be relevant to the authority assessment but does not by itself settle every downstream capture or processing question. Multi-party presence alone is not a failure, and a valid basis that independently covers the affected participant and use defeats the threshold.

failure_classification.likelihood: demonstrated across multiple AI meeting-assistant allegations and independently reported third-party webinar capture; prevalence and legal outcomes remain unresolved
failure_classification.confidence: high mechanism confidence; some incident particulars remain allegations or context-dependent
failure_classification.failure_scope: multi-party human interactions where one person's use or technical access to an AI-enabled capture system affects another person's identifiable contribution
failure_classification.recurrence_pattern: likely wherever AI assistants or capture services are introduced into shared interactions without participant-aware authority handling
failure_classification.persistence: can persist across repeated meetings, standing bots, workplace integrations, classrooms, webinars, conferences, support groups, service calls and institutional deployments
failure_classification.reproducibility: testable with multi-party scenarios that vary user/non-user status, public or discoverable links, notice, consent, public/private setting, minors, biometrics, confidentiality and representative authority
failure_classification.visibility: partly user-visible through bot presence, notices and product controls; covert or third-party capture can make the relevant authority state opaque to affected participants
failure_classification.severity_assessment_basis: S2 reflects repeated cross-vendor and cross-context evidence affecting privacy, biometric, workplace, health/support-group and non-user interests without current evidence of catastrophic or irreversible population-scale harm.
failure_classification.severity_assessment_gap: Jurisdiction-specific legal requirements, provider configurations, prevalence and final litigation outcomes remain unresolved.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The core mechanism is transposition of authority from one human participant, organiser or access holder to another affected participant whose contribution requires an independently adequate authority determination.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Authority tied to one principal is carried into another principal's contribution without fresh validation.
